Compute IDM Cuts from a Cumulative Ordinal Model

computeCutsIDMOrdinal.Rd

Estimates all performance-level boundaries jointly with a cumulative-logit model. By default, crossed random intercepts account for systematic differences between raters and between items. The main cuts describe a reference rater and item whose random intercepts are zero. Input columns follow the conventions of computeCutsIDMMAPT.

Usage

computeCutsIDMOrdinal(
  dat,
  boundaries = c(1.5, 2.5, 3.5, 4.5),
  est_col = "est",
  item_id_col = NULL,
  rater_cols = NULL,
  rater_pattern = "Rater",
  rater_id_col = NULL,
  rating_col = NULL,
  input_format = c("auto", "long", "wide"),
  rating_levels = NULL,
  missing = c("drop", "error"),
  cut_labels = NULL,
  per_rater = TRUE,
  random_effects = c("rater", "item"),
  control = list()
)

Arguments

dat

A data frame containing item difficulties and ordered ratings. Each item–rater pair must occur at most once, and an item must have the same difficulty wherever it occurs.

boundaries

Strictly increasing half-integers selecting adjacent rating levels, for example c(1.5, 2.5) for three levels. These are indices on the rating scale, not item difficulties. When omitted together with explicit rating_levels, all adjacent boundaries are returned. With the category definition held fixed, selecting fewer boundaries changes only the returned cuts. See rating_levels for how boundaries also enter the category definition when labels are not supplied.

est_col

Name of the finite, nonmissing numeric item-difficulty column. The returned cuts use this same scale.

item_id_col

Name of the item identifier column. Required for long input. With wide input, rows identify items when this argument is omitted.

rater_cols

Names of the rating columns in wide input. If NULL, they are selected by rater_pattern.

rater_pattern

Regular expression identifying wide rating columns.

rater_id_col

Name of the rater identifier column in long input.

rating_col

Name of the rating column in long input.

input_format

"long" requires item, rater, and rating columns. "wide" uses one row per item and one column per rater. "auto" infers the layout from the supplied column arguments.

rating_levels

Optional unique rating labels ordered from lowest to highest performance level, for example c("1a", "1b", "2", "3") or c("basic", "proficient", "advanced"). Their positions become indices 1, ..., K. Without this argument, ratings must be positive integer level codes, and the declared levels are 1, ..., K, where K is the largest observed code or ceiling(boundaries), whichever is greater. The default boundaries therefore declare at least five levels. Supply rating_levels to fix the category definition independently of the requested output boundaries.

missing

"drop" removes missing ratings while keeping other available ratings of the same item or rater. "error" rejects missing ratings. Missing identifiers and difficulties are always rejected.

cut_labels

Optional unique, nonempty names for the requested cuts. Defaults to names such as cut12, or cut_basic_proficient with explicit category labels. The name "person" is reserved.

per_rater

Also return conditional rater cuts? Defaults to TRUE. They use the rater effects estimated in the same joint model; no separate rater models are fitted. This argument does not change the reference cuts or the estimated model.

random_effects

Character vector selecting random intercepts: c("rater", "item") (default), "rater", "item", or character() for a model without random effects. Selected grouping factors must have enough observed groups and replication to fit their effects. The function does not silently remove a requested effect.

control

Named list of supported optimization controls. Both model types accept trace, maxIter, gradTol, and maxLineIter. Mixed models additionally accept innerCtrl, useMatrix, checkRanef, and the nlminb controls iter.max, eval.max, rel.tol, abs.tol, x.tol, xf.tol, step.min, step.max, sing.tol, and diff.g. Models without random effects also accept relTol, tol, maxModIter, and convergence. See clmm.control, clm.control, and nlminb. The optimizer is fixed to nlminb for mixed models and Newton for models without random effects; unsupported controls cause an error. Mixed-model defaults include useMatrix = TRUE, maxIter = 100, innerCtrl = "giveError", iter.max = 200, eval.max = 400, and rel.tol = 1e-10.

Details

Methodological basis and scope

This function applies an established ordinal modelling framework to IDM ratings. Christensen's (2026) cumulative-link mixed-model tutorial gives the cumulative-logit model with normally distributed judge effects, and the ordinal documentation supports crossed random effects. Taylor et al. (2023), especially their Simulation 2, motivate modelling ordinal item ratings with both participant and item effects. Their application concerns rating norms and uses a probit link; this function uses a logit link. Their study does not address IDM standard setting.

For IDM itself, Ferrara et al. (2008, p. 12) describe logistic regression as one way of locating cuts in transition regions. Sireci et al. (2006, pp. 54–55) derive MAPT cuts from separate binary regressions at probability 0.5. The present function combines the ordinal mixed-model framework with this probability-crossing definition, estimating all boundaries jointly. The cited works support these ingredients; they do not establish this particular combination as a validated or superior IDM cut-score method. The formulas below specify the package's extension explicitly.

1. Ordered ratings and the difficulty scale

Let \(i\) index items, \(r\) raters, and \(R_{ir}\in\{1,\ldots,K\}\) the ordered rating assigned to an item. The response is a rating category, not whether a student answers correctly. With rating_levels = c("basic", "proficient", "advanced"), the indices are 1, 2, and 3. A requested boundary \(b_k=k+0.5\) separates categories at or below \(k\) from those above \(k\); for example, boundaries = 1.5 separates basic from the higher categories. These boundary indices differ from both fitted model thresholds and cuts on the item-difficulty scale.

Write \(\mathcal O\) for the set of retained item–rater pairs and \(N=|\mathcal O|\) for the number of observed ratings. Each item has one supplied difficulty \(x_i\). For numerical stability, the function uses standardized difficulties $$ \mu=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{(i,r)\in\mathcal O}x_i,\qquad s=\sqrt{\frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{(i,r)\in\mathcal O}(x_i-\mu)^2},\qquad z_i=\frac{x_i-\mu}{s}. $$ An item's difficulty enters these summaries once per observed rating. Thus items with more ratings contribute more entries when the design is unbalanced. Returned cuts are transformed back to the original scale.

2. Cumulative probabilities and proportional odds

Define the logistic distribution function \(\Lambda(t)=1/(1+\exp(-t))\) and the linear predictor \(\eta_{ir}=\beta z_i+u_r+v_i\). The model is $$ \Pr(R_{ir}\leq k\mid x_i,u_r,v_i)=\Lambda(\alpha_k-\eta_{ir}), \qquad k=1,\ldots,K-1. $$ Equivalently, since \(\operatorname{logit}(p)=\log(p/(1-p))\), $$ \operatorname{logit}\Pr(R_{ir}\leq k\mid x_i,u_r,v_i) =\alpha_k-\beta z_i-u_r-v_i. $$ Here \(\alpha_1<\cdots<\alpha_{K-1}\) are freely estimated thresholds on the latent logit scale, \(\beta\) is the common difficulty slope, and \(u_r\) and \(v_i\) are rater and item random intercepts. There is no separate fixed intercept: its location is absorbed into the thresholds. Their spacings are not constrained to be equal.

The upper-category probability used for the cuts is $$ p_k(x_i,u_r,v_i)=\Pr(R_{ir}>k\mid x_i,u_r,v_i) =\Lambda(\beta z_i+u_r+v_i-\alpha_k). $$ The same \(\beta\) applies to every boundary. Holding the random effects fixed, an increase of \(\Delta x\) in difficulty multiplies the odds of a rating above any boundary by \(\exp(\beta\Delta x/s)\). This is the proportional-odds assumption. A positive slope makes these probabilities increase with difficulty.

3. Category probabilities, random effects, and estimation

The model uses the full ordered response in one likelihood. Define \(\alpha_0=-\infty\) and \(\alpha_K=+\infty\). The probability of a particular category \(j\) is the difference between two cumulative probabilities: $$ \pi_{irj}=\Pr(R_{ir}=j\mid x_i,u_r,v_i) =\Lambda(\alpha_j-\eta_{ir})-\Lambda(\alpha_{j-1}-\eta_{ir}), \qquad j=1,\ldots,K. $$ These probabilities are nonnegative and sum to one. For a fixed category definition, changing which boundaries are requested for output does not change the categories used in the fit or create separate regressions.

The random intercepts satisfy $$ u_r\sim N(0,\sigma_u^2),\qquad v_i\sim N(0,\sigma_v^2). $$ They are mutually independent and independent of the supplied difficulty predictor. Ratings are assumed conditionally independent given these effects. Sharing a rater or an item nevertheless induces dependence after the effects are integrated out. The effects are crossed when raters assess multiple items and items are assessed by multiple raters.

Let \(\phi_{\sigma}\) denote a mean-zero normal density with standard deviation \(\sigma\). For positive variance components, the marginal likelihood is $$ L(\boldsymbol{\alpha},\beta,\sigma_u,\sigma_v) =\int\!\int \left[\prod_{(i,r)\in\mathcal O}\pi_{ir,R_{ir}}\right] \left[\prod_r\phi_{\sigma_u}(u_r)\right] \left[\prod_i\phi_{\sigma_v}(v_i)\right] \,d\boldsymbol{u}\,d\boldsymbol{v}. $$ The integration is over all observed rater and item effects, not separately over each rating. The thresholds, common slope, and variance components are estimated jointly by approximate maximum likelihood using clmm with link = "logit", flexible thresholds, and the Laplace approximation (nAGQ = 1). Omitted effects are fixed to zero and their integrals disappear. A zero variance component is interpreted as a degenerate distribution at zero. With no random effects, clm maximizes the ordinary ordinal likelihood.

The returned random-effect estimates are conditional modes given the fitted model parameters. For positive fitted variances they maximize, up to constants, $$ \sum_{(i,r)\in\mathcal O}\log\pi_{ir,R_{ir}} -\frac{1}{2\widehat\sigma_u^2}\sum_r u_r^2 -\frac{1}{2\widehat\sigma_v^2}\sum_i v_i^2. $$ The normal-distribution terms shrink the effects towards zero. A positive rater effect means a tendency to assign higher levels at the same difficulty; a positive item effect means higher ratings for that item than its supplied difficulty alone predicts. Item effects describe residual variation in ratings, not measurement error or recalibration of est. Ratings are not smoothed or automatically trimmed.

4. Deriving reference cuts at probability 0.5

Use hats to denote estimated model parameters. The reference probability curve fixes both random intercepts to zero: $$ \widehat p_k(x,0,0) =\Lambda\left(\widehat\beta\frac{x-\mu}{s}-\widehat\alpha_k\right). $$ A reference cut \(\widehat c_k\) satisfies \(\widehat p_k(\widehat c_k,0,0)=0.5\). Because \(\operatorname{logit}(0.5)=0\), $$ \widehat\beta\frac{\widehat c_k-\mu}{s}-\widehat\alpha_k=0 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad \widehat c_k=\mu+s\frac{\widehat\alpha_k}{\widehat\beta}. $$ These values appear in cuts_summary. They are difficulties, whereas \(\widehat\alpha_k\) is a threshold on the model's latent scale. The 0.5 criterion concerns a rating-level assignment; it is neither a student's probability of answering correctly nor the proportion of the student population above a cut. It also does not by itself establish a classification rule with optimal educational consequences.

With \(s>0\), \(\widehat\beta>0\), and ordered thresholds, $$ \widehat c_{k+1}-\widehat c_k =\frac{s}{\widehat\beta}(\widehat\alpha_{k+1}-\widehat\alpha_k)>0. $$ Thus the joint model supplies ordered cuts without sorting the estimated values after fitting.

5. Conditional rater cuts and the plotted curves

For rater \(r\), retain the estimated conditional mode \(\widehat u_r\) and set the item effect to zero. Solving \(\widehat p_k(x,\widehat u_r,0)=0.5\) gives $$ \widehat c_{rk} =\mu+s\frac{\widehat\alpha_k-\widehat u_r}{\widehat\beta} =\widehat c_k-\frac{s\widehat u_r}{\widehat\beta}. $$ These are cuts_per_person. A positive rater effect shifts all of that rater's cuts down by the same amount; random slopes or rater-specific threshold spacings are not fitted. The estimates come from one shared model, not independent rater fits. With no rater effect, observed raters share the reference cuts. Raters without retained ratings have no individual cut.

For \(u^*=0\) in the reference panel, or \(u^*=\widehat u_r\) in a rater panel, the displayed curve can also be written on the original difficulty scale as $$ \widehat p_k(x,u^*,0)=\Lambda(A_k+B x),\qquad A_k=u^*-\widehat\alpha_k-\widehat\beta\mu/s,\qquad B=\widehat\beta/s. $$ The diagnostic columns intercept and slope contain \(A_k\) and \(B\); equivalently the curve is \(\Lambda(B(x-\widehat c))\). Item effects are estimated and returned, but held at zero in all reported cuts and plotted curves.

The reference cuts are not obtained by averaging the fitted rater cuts. Nor is the reference probability curve a marginal curve averaged over raters and items. Under the assumed symmetric, mean-zero random-effect distributions, the model-population marginal curve does share its 0.5 crossing with the reference curve: at that point the logistic argument is \(u+v\), and \(\Lambda(t)+\Lambda(-t)=1\). Their shapes still differ when the random-effect variance is positive. This identity does not require an empirical, possibly unbalanced average of the observed raters and items to have the same crossing.

6. Worked numerical example

Suppose difficulties were standardized with \(\mu=500\), \(s=100\), and the fitted four-category model has \(\widehat\beta=2\) and \((\widehat\alpha_1,\widehat\alpha_2,\widehat\alpha_3)=(-1,0,1)\). For boundaries 1.5, 2.5, and 3.5, the reference cuts are $$ 500+100\frac{(-1,0,1)}{2}=(450,500,550). $$ For a rater with \(\widehat u_r=0.4\), the cuts shift by \(-100\times0.4/2=-20\), giving \((430,480,530)\). For the middle boundary, the rater's upper-category logit at difficulty 480 is \(2(480-500)/100+0.4-0=0\), so its probability is exactly 0.5. The corresponding reference probability is 0.5 at difficulty 500. These numbers illustrate the calculation; they are not empirical results.

Fit diagnostics and unavailable cuts

Inspect model_diagnostics and cut_diagnostics before using the cuts. The common difficulty slope must be positive and numerically nonzero. A failed, nonconverged, or otherwise unusable model yields NA cuts and an explanatory diagnostic status, with the original rating data retained. Invalid input instead produces an error.

Every declared category must occur in the retained ratings. With at least two observed categories, an unobserved declared category gives missing_categories diagnostics and unavailable cuts; the function does not silently join categories and relabel the remaining thresholds. For a fixed category definition, requesting only a subset of boundaries does not remove this requirement because the same joint ordinal model is still fitted. The statuses are:

ok

A usable fit and positive common slope supply cuts.

one_class

Fewer than two categories occur in the retained ratings.

missing_categories

Some declared categories are unobserved.

constant_est

All retained item difficulties are identical.

separation

The difficulty ranges of successive categories are completely ordered without overlap, allowing an infinite increasing slope.

nonpositive_slope

The common slope is nonpositive or numerically flat.

non_convergence

The optimizer or subsequent gradient checks do not establish convergence.

ill_conditioned

Hessian checks do not establish adequate curvature for the estimated parameters.

unordered_thresholds

Estimated thresholds are not strictly ordered.

fit_error, non_finite

Estimation failed or returned unusable numerical values; inspect the stored warning.

no_data

An individual rater has no retained ratings.

The numerical diagnostics include convergence information, raw and Hessian-scaled maximum absolute gradients, Hessian information, and a flag for random-effect standard deviations below \(10^{-4}\). A near-zero variance may indicate that the data support little residual variation for that grouping factor; it does not by itself invalidate otherwise usable cuts. A usable model does not establish that the proportional-odds or random-effect assumptions hold. When a variance lies at its zero boundary and the stored Hessian is ill-conditioned, the function checks the Hessian and gradient after removing only the variance dimensions whose standard deviations are below \(10^{-4}\). Fixed parameters and other variance dimensions remain in this check. The original stored-Hessian diagnostic remains available; ordinal may itself have already removed boundary dimensions.

Cuts outside the observed difficulty range are retained and marked extrapolated = TRUE. Reference cuts use the overall observed range; individual diagnostics use the corresponding rater's observed range. With a usable positive slope and ordered thresholds, the requested cuts are ordered. The function does not rearrange estimates to hide a failed fit.

Plotting and interpretation

plotCutsIDM(result, show_aggregate = TRUE) shows conditional rater curves and the Reference (ordinal) panel. Curves show \(\Pr(R>k\mid x)\) with the item effect fixed to zero; the reference panel also sets the rater effect to zero. With per_rater = FALSE, only the reference panel is shown. Plotting uses the stored fit results and does not estimate new models.

Raw points show observed proportions above each boundary. Optional residuals are the differences between these proportions and the displayed curves. Because the displayed curves set item effects to zero, these are reference-curve discrepancies rather than residuals from the fully conditional model.

plotPopulationCutsIDM accepts the result directly. Its legacy cut_selection = "mean" option selects reference cuts; "both" adds the conditional rater cuts. plotWrightMap also accepts the result through cuts, using cuts_summary. Plausible values and item difficulties must already share the same metric.

Limits of the calculation

This model respects the order of rating categories without treating their numerical codes as equally spaced. Its shared slope is more restrictive than fitting a separate binary regression at each boundary. Assess the proportional-odds assumption, the pattern of rater and item effects, and sensitivity to influential observations before adopting cuts.

No cut-score confidence intervals are computed. Standard errors in the stored model concern the fitted model and treat the input difficulties as known. They do not propagate item-calibration uncertainty, dependence created by panel discussion, or other sources of uncertainty outside this model. A small variance component or a precise model fit is not evidence that the performance-level descriptors are substantively valid.

Value

A list of class cutsIDMOrdinal, including:

cuts_summary

One-row tibble of reference cuts, with columns named by cut_labels, on the original item-difficulty scale.

cuts_per_person

Conditional rater cuts, with a person column followed by the cut columns; NULL when per_rater = FALSE.

cut_diagnostics, diagnostics_per_person

Diagnostic tables for the reference and conditional rater cuts. They identify each boundary and cut, its status, warnings, and whether it lies outside the observed range. n, n_lower, and n_upper count retained ratings, not unique items. threshold is the selected model threshold on the standardized latent scale. intercept and slope describe the displayed upper-category logit on the original difficulty scale: \(\operatorname{logit}\Pr(R>k)=\text{intercept}+\text{slope}\,x\). The reference has rater_effect = 0; individual rows retain their conditional rater effect. min_est and max_est give the observed range used to flag extrapolation. Individual diagnostics are NULL when per_rater = FALSE.

model

The fitted clmm or clm object when available. Its predictor difficulty uses the internal standardized scale. model$est_center and model$est_scale retain the transformation parameters. The model may remain available even when its diagnostics make the resulting cuts unusable.

model_diagnostics

One-row tibble with status, converged, max_gradient, max_scaled_gradient, hessian_positive_definite, condition_number, singular, and warning, as well as est_center, est_scale, and counts n_ratings, n_items, and n_raters. Unavailable diagnostic quantities are NA.

rater_effects, item_effects

Estimated conditional random intercepts in effect, with identifiers person or item_id and retained-rating counts n. Effects are on the latent logit scale, not on the item-difficulty scale. Excluded effect terms have zero effects for observed groups. Groups with no retained ratings have NA effects.

variance_components

Grouping factor, variance, standard deviation, and number of observed groups for the requested random intercepts.

data_used

Retained long-format rating data with item_id, person, est, stage_label, and stage_raw.

n_dropped

Number of missing ratings removed.

boundaries, rating_levels, cut_labels

Requested boundaries, ordered category labels, and output column names.

cuts_ordered

Whether all reference cuts are strictly increasing; NA if any is unavailable.

random_effects, control, method

Requested random-effect terms, supplied optimizer controls, and a description of the fitted method.

input_format, est_col, item_id_col, rater_id_col, rating_col, missing

Input layout and column/missing-value settings.

See also

computeCutsIDM, computeCutsIDMMAPT, summary.cutsIDMOrdinal, plotCutsIDM, plotPopulationCutsIDM, clmm

References

Christensen, R. H. B. (2026). A Tutorial on fitting Cumulative Link Mixed Models with clmm2 from the ordinal Package. Package vignette, version dated July 26, 2026. See Equation (1) and pp. 1–2 for the cumulative-logit model with normal judge effects and Laplace estimation, and pp. 5–6 for conditional modes and reference predictions. https://stat.ethz.ch/CRAN/web/packages/ordinal/vignettes/clmm2_tutorial.pdf. For crossed random effects in the current clmm implementation, see ordinal: Regression Models for Ordinal Data, doi:10.32614/CRAN.package.ordinal , and https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/ordinal/refman/ordinal.html#clmm.

Taylor, J. E., Rousselet, G. A., Scheepers, C., and Sereno, S. C. (2023). Rating norms should be calculated from cumulative link mixed effects models. Behavior Research Methods, 55, 2175–2196. doi:10.3758/s13428-022-01814-7 . See “Simulation 2: CLMMs with item and participant random effects” for ordinal ratings with both item and participant effects.

Ferrara, S., Perie, M., and Johnson, E. (2008). Matching the judgmental task with standard setting panelist expertise: The Item-Descriptor (ID) Matching Method. Journal of Applied Testing Technology, 9(1). See p. 12 for logistic regression as an IDM cut-location method. https://www.testpublishers.org/assets/documents/Issue%201%202008.pdf.

Sireci, S. G., Baldwin, P., Martone, A., Zenisky Laguilles, A., Hambleton, R. K., and Han, K. T. (2006). Massachusetts Adult Proficiency Tests Technical Manual. Center for Educational Assessment Research Report No. 600, University of Massachusetts Amherst. See pp. 54–55 for separate binary logistic regressions and the probability-0.5 cut definition used in MAPT standard setting. https://bpb-us-e2.wpmucdn.com/websites.umass.edu/dist/5/40195/files/2021/03/MAPT_TechnicalManualv1.pdf.

Examples

## Simulated ratings with rater and item variation.
set.seed(4721)
n_items <- 60L
n_raters <- 10L
ratings <- expand.grid(item = seq_len(n_items), rater = seq_len(n_raters))
ratings$est <- seq(-3.5, 3.5, length.out = n_items)[ratings$item]
rater_shift <- rnorm(n_raters, sd = 0.7)
item_shift <- rnorm(n_items, sd = 0.65)
latent <- 1.1 * ratings$est + rater_shift[ratings$rater] +
  item_shift[ratings$item] + rlogis(nrow(ratings))
ratings$rating <- findInterval(latent, c(-1.5, -0.5, 0.5, 1.5)) + 1L

mixed_cuts <- computeCutsIDMOrdinal(
  ratings, item_id_col = "item", rater_id_col = "rater",
  rating_col = "rating", rating_levels = 1:5
)
mixed_cuts$cuts_summary
#> # A tibble: 1 × 4
#>   cut_1_2 cut_2_3 cut_3_4 cut_4_5
#>     <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>
#> 1   -1.35  -0.418   0.487    1.55
mixed_cuts$variance_components
#> # A tibble: 2 × 4
#>   group variance    sd n_levels
#>   <chr>    <dbl> <dbl>    <int>
#> 1 rater    0.844 0.919       10
#> 2 item     0.748 0.865       60
head(mixed_cuts$rater_effects)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 3
#>   person  effect     n
#>   <chr>    <dbl> <int>
#> 1 1       0.564     60
#> 2 10      0.0523    60
#> 3 2       0.204     60
#> 4 3      -0.924     60
#> 5 4      -1.21      60
#> 6 5      -0.204     60
summary(mixed_cuts, per_rater = TRUE)
#> Joint ordinal IDM cuts (cumulative logit)
#> 600 ratings from 10 raters on 60 items; 0 missing ratings dropped.
#> Random intercepts: rater, item 
#> 
#> Reference cuts (rater and item effects set to zero):
#>  cut_name    cut status extrapolated

#>   cut_2_3 -0.418     ok        FALSE
#>   cut_3_4  0.487     ok        FALSE
#>   cut_4_5  1.554     ok        FALSE
#> 
#> Model diagnostics:
#>  status converged max_gradient max_scaled_gradient hessian_positive_definite
#>      ok      TRUE        0.001                   0                      TRUE
#>  singular warning
#>     FALSE        
#> 
#> Random-intercept variance components (logit scale):
#>  group variance    sd n_levels
#>  rater    0.844 0.919       10
#>   item    0.748 0.865       60
#> 
#> Conditional rater cuts (joint fit, item effect set to zero):
#>  person cut_1_2 cut_2_3 cut_3_4 cut_4_5
#>       1  -1.870  -0.936  -0.032   1.035
#>      10  -1.400  -0.466   0.439   1.506
#>       2  -1.539  -0.605   0.299   1.366
#>       3  -0.501   0.433   1.337   2.404
#>       4  -0.235   0.699   1.603   2.670
#>       5  -1.164  -0.230   0.675   1.742
#>       6  -0.197   0.737   1.642   2.708

## The same data in wide format use the same item and category definitions.
wide_ratings <- tidyr::pivot_wider(
  ratings, id_cols = c(item, est), names_from = rater,
  values_from = rating, names_prefix = "Rater"
)
wide_cuts <- computeCutsIDMOrdinal(
  wide_ratings, item_id_col = "item", rating_levels = 1:5
)

## A small fixed-effects comparison, without random intercepts:
dat <- data.frame(
  est = 1:12,
  RaterA = c(1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 1, 2),
  RaterB = c(1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 2, 1, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2)
)
cuts <- computeCutsIDMOrdinal(dat, rating_levels = c(1, 2),
                              random_effects = character())
cuts$cuts_summary
#> # A tibble: 1 × 1
#>   cut_1_2
#>     <dbl>
#> 1     6.5
cuts$cut_diagnostics
#> # A tibble: 1 × 16
#>   cut_name boundary   cut     n n_lower n_upper min_est max_est threshold
#>   <chr>       <dbl> <dbl> <int>   <int>   <int>   <int>   <int>     <dbl>
#> 1 cut_1_2       1.5   6.5    24      12      12       1      12  2.22e-16
#> # ℹ 7 more variables: intercept <dbl>, slope <dbl>, rater_effect <dbl>,
#> #   converged <lgl>, extrapolated <lgl>, status <chr>, warning <chr>
plotCutsIDM(cuts, show_aggregate = TRUE, cut_value_digits = 2)
